lawyer:
Golam Kibria. Deputy Attorney-General with Md Jamil Akhter Elahi, Assistant Attorney-Genera-For the State. 
Md Anowarul Islam. Advocate-State Defence Lawyer. 
Abdul Malek, Senior Advocate with AM Mahbub Uddin Khokan,  SM Shahjahan and Md Ariful Islam. Advocates-For the Condemned Prisoner/Appellant Uzzal alias Elias Hossain ..
parties:
Uzzal alias Elias Hossain ------ Condemned Prisoner-Appellant
Vs.
State ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
7. Upon consideration of the evidence and materials on record, including the deposition of the witnesses the learned trial Judge convicted all the accused persons sentencing them as stated above. 

 8. Mr Golam Kibria, learned Deputy Attorney-General, having taken us through the First Information Report, deposition of the witnesses and other evidence and materials on record, made his submissions on behalf of the State in favour of confirmation of the sentence of death awarded by the learned trial Judge. He submitted that although the nature of the case is Such that no direct evidence can be expected as there was no eye witness of the occurrence, there was sufficient corroborative evidence by way of testimony of the other witnesses who deposed in Court narrating the incidence of rape committed upon the victim Mahima who subsequently, as a result of the activities of the rapists, committed suicide by taking poison. Elaborating his submissions further, the learned Deputy Attorney-General sought to impress upon us the fact that after the occurrence of rape the victim's father went to the parents of the rapists and sought from them justice and return of the indecent photographs which had been taken of his dalighter as well as the negatives. He submitted that the appearance of the parents and guardians of the accused persons along with the accused persons at the house of the informant on the following day and the use of abusive language and their accusation that the informant's daughter was of immoral character and their failure to return the photographs and negative were all activities which led to the death of the victim, albeit by committing suicide. He submitted that such activities of the accused and also of their parents and guardians are sufficient for the purpose of conviction under section 9(2) of the Ain. He further submitted that the fact that the victim was raped is proved by the evidence of the victim's parents and siblings as well as immediate neighbours who heard directly from the victim, that she was raped by the accused persons and this fact has been corroborated by the post-mortem examination and the evidence given in Court by all 3 members of the Board of Doctors who conducted the postmortem examination. The learned Deputy Attorney-General said that the statement of Mahima narrated to her relatives and deposed by them in Court is admissible under section 60 of the Evidence Act read with illustration (j) of section 8 and section 32 of the said Act. He submitted that the narration of the event of rape and the circumstances which led to the victim's death are relevant. In this regard he referred to Dr Jainand and. another vs Rex, AIR (36) 1949 Allahabad 291. He also referred to SM Qamruzzaman vs State 33 PLR 156 and submitted that the statements upon which certain action was taken and certain results followed will be admissible. He also submit- ted that Mahima's statements is admissible as statement under section 3 of the Evidence Act as narrated by her father and other relatives. He also added that the mental torture suffered by the victim as a result of the subsequent acts of rebuke and abuse by the accused persons and their parents/ guardians led to Mahima's death. 

 10. Mr Abdul Malek and Mr SM Shahjahan, appeared with Mr AM Mahbub Uddin, learned Advocate engaged by the condemned prisoner/ appellant Uzzal alias Elias Hossain. They submitted that the death of the victim was not as a result of the rape since the evidence on record clearly shows that she committed suicide 4 days after the alleged occurrence of rape by taking poison. The learned Advocate also refuted the contention that the subsequent acts of the accused persons led to the suicide and hence the question of any offence under sections 9(2) or 9(3) of the Ain does not arise. He elaborated by submitting that in order to come under the provisions of section 9(2) of the Ain the death must be the natural consequence of the acts of the rapists and clearly in the facts of the instant case the death having been by way of suicide, the conviction of the accused under section 9(2) cannot be sustained. 

 11. Moreover, the learned Advocate submitted that at the time of drafting that section the legislature did not foresee the possibility of death by suicide after the event of death and consequently, section 9(Ka) of the Ain was added in 2003. But since that provision did not exist at the time of com- mission of the offence alleged, no conviction can be based on the law promulgated subsequently. The learned Advocate pointed out that although the allegation is of rape and the post mortem examination report shows injuries on the body of the victim, which would otherwise be sufficient for an offence under section 9(3), in the facts of the instant case, he submitted, neither rape nor the injuries on the victim have been proved by cogent evidence. The learned Advocate pointed out further that although the rape is alleged to have been committed on 15-2-2002, no information of any kind was filed with any authority until 19-2-2002 and at no point in time was there any allegation that any injury was inflicted upon the victim during the course of the alleged rape. He further pointed out that even at the time of the inquest PW 7, a close relative of the victim, was present, who himself stated that he was told about the occurrence and the names of the accused had been disclosed to him on the date of the occurrence, did not mention the names of the accused at the time of the inquest, which he witnessed. The learned Advocate pointed out also that at the time of the inquest the dead body was turned and inspected with the help of the victim's maternal grandmother, but no injury was found on her person. Hence evidence of any rape or injury caused by the accused is totally absent. 

 12. With regard to subsequent activities, the learned Advocate submitted that the first information report does not disclose any such activities by the accused or their parents/guardians and therefore, it is a subsequent embellishment, as is the introduction of alleged injuries, which were neither mentioned in the first information report nor in the inquest report nor mentioned by any of the witnesses apart from PW 8, herself did not say so in her examination-in-chief nor in her statement to the police made under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The learned Advocate emphatically submitted that the alleged injuries were subsequently introduced at the behest of the informant party and to that extent the post-mortem report is false. He further supported his contention by  pointing out that the injuries allegedly were present at the time of the post mortem examination which took place 4 days after the event and would, therefore, have been serious injuries, but there is no evidence of any treatment having been received by the victim during the period between receiving the injuries and her death. The learned Advocate pointed out that allegedly the rape took place in a sugarcane field and she had been stripped naked at the time of the rape and, therefore, the absence of any scratch marks or other injuries on her back or buttocks belies the allegation of rape. 

 13. The learned Advocate further pointed out that the prosecution failed to call as witness the informant's mother who, according to the evidence of other witnesses, lived in a hut on the same compound and also failed to produce as prosecution witness Sobhan and Kalam. Learned Advocate further pointed out that PWs 2, 3, 7 and 10 deposed that they heard about the incident from PW 1, but the informant (PW 1) did not state in his deposition about his narration of the story to PWs 2,3,7 and 10. He submitted that, therefore, the evidence of PWs 2, 3, 7 and 10 is inadmissible and ought not to have been admitted as evidence by the learned trial Judge. He further pointed out that PW 2 named the alleged accused persons but did not name the .appellant Uzzal and, therefore, the conviction of the appellant cannot be sustained. 

 15. Finally, the learned Advocate submitted that the evidence of the doctors who conducted the post mortem examination can only be treated as corroborative evidence to corroborate the evidence of other witnesses; their evidence cannot be substantive evidence. He pointed out that since the other witnesses did not mention any injury on the person of the victim, the evidence of the doctors in this regard must be left out of consideration, He submitted that, therefore, there being no direct evidence or circumstantial evidence against the accused persons, the conviction and sentence cannot be sustained and prayed that the appellant be acquitted of the charges leveled against him. 

 16. Mr Md Anowarul Islam, learned Advocate appearing as State Defence on behalf of the 3 absconding convicts, submitted that the implication of the accused persons in the case is totally due to their political affiliation and as result of grudge due to the demolition of the club house. He further submitted that the prosecution did not prove that the occurrence took place in the sugarcane field. He submitted that the conviction is based totally on hearsay evidence and, therefore, cannot be sustained. With regard to the delay in lodging the first information report, he cited Ghulam and others vs State, 1983 PCrLJ 196. He submitted that the delay in lodging the first information report creates a doubt in the prosecution case. Moreover, there were no independent witnesses in the case and, therefore, the conviction and sentence should be set aside. 

 17. Now let us consider the evidence in the case. Md Abdul Hannan, the informant deposing as PW 1, narrated how the accused Farid, Faroque, Selim and Uzzal, who Were armed with hashua, chora and knife, etc, having tied a gamcha to. her mouth, abducted his minor daughter Mahima from his compound and took her to the nearby sugarcane field where they undressed her and raped her one after another. Accused Farid took photographs of his daughter when Selim was raping her. Mahima then came home crying and narrated the occurrence to her younger sister Fahima and her mother when she returned home. When the witness returned home from Taherpur hat at 9-00 PM he was told of the occurrence by his wife, Mahima and his younger daughter. He stated that he advised them to remain calm and that he went and informed the father/guardians of the accused persons about the occurrence demanding from them justice and the return of the photographs and negatives. But since his requests and begging did not bear any fruit, his daughter Mahima, in order to save her honour and self-respect, took poison at about 11-30 AM on 19-2-2002. She was immediately admitted to Putia Hospital where she died at about 1-00 PM while under treatment. The witness identified his signature on the first information report which was marked as Exhibit 1/1, Mahima's dead body was sent to Rajshahi Medical College Hospital for post mortem examination. He also stated that at the time of investigation, the investigating officer (IO) took from him a hand written letter and envelope and the wearing apparel of Mahima, He stated further that witnesses Sobhan and Kamal had been gained over by the accused and would not depose in the case he identified accused Uzzal in the dock and stated that the other accused persons were absconding. In his cross-examination, he stated that he went to the market at 1-00 PM on the date of occurrence in order to purchase a head of cattle for Qurbani (sacrifice). He was accompanied by Aslam when he heard about the occurrence from his wife, Mahima and Fahima. He also stated that his mother used to stay in the south facing 'Chhapra hat.' He stated further that on the date of occurrence his wife had gone to the house of his brother Mannan at about 4-30/5-00 PM and Mahima and Fahima had gone to watch TV and Mahima returned home at about 4-00 PM and Fahima stayed behind to Watch TV up to about 10 minutes before Magrib. He stated that when he returned home he first heard the story from his wife and then spoke to Mahima, Fahima and his son. He did not inform the Members/Chairman about the occurrence nor filed any GD at the police station, but informed the village headman Aslam and Matabbor Abdul Aziz. He did not inform any others for fear of dishonour, He admitted that after Mahima committed suicide by taking poison he lodged another case against the parents and guardians of the accused persons. He could not say where Mahima had obtained the poison nor recovered the bottle containing poison. She was taken to Putia Hospital about one kilometre away. He stated that witness Sobhan was his cousin and also maternal grandfather of Uzzal, but denied the suggestion that on the date of occurrence Kalarn and Sobhan were crushing sugarcane in his sugarcane mill. In his further cross-examination he stated that PW 5, Jahangir is his son, PW 4, Lutfor is his neighbour, PW 8, Sanowara is his wife, PW 6, Fahima is his daughter, PW 7, Wahed is his paternal cousin, PW 3, Anowar is his nephew by his paternal cousin and PW 10, Mannan is his elder brother. He also stated that Razzak is his paternal uncle. He denied the suggestion that there was a case Pending between him and Abdus Samad who was the maternal uncle-in-law of Uzzal's father and that there was existing enmity between him and Uzzal's family. He denied the defence suggestion that he and his son were involved in the construction of a club house which was used for anti-social activities and was demolished upon an application filed by accused Uzzal and his father before the Upazila Nirbahi Officer for which the informant swore to take revenge. He denied that defence suggestion that he was affiliated to any political party or that Uzzal was affiliated to any political party. He admitted that ex-prime minister Sheikh Hasina visited his house after the occurrence and that the Home Minister and local Member of Parliament, Mayor of the City Corporation, DIG of Police and may others visited his house. He admitted that Advocate Jamshed wrote the first information report, but stated that he did, not know if he was connected with Awami League. He denied the suggestion that Uzzal had been implicated in the case due to political rivalry, He denied the suggestion that he did not state in the first information report that he did not inform the occurrence to the parents and guardians of the accused persons. He admitted that he was present at the hospital when Mahima died, but could not remember when the police went there. He denied the suggestion that Mahima had an affair with a boy of his village and because he refused to give her in marriage to him she committed suicide and that he concocted the Whole story against the accused persons upon being influenced by various people. In his further cross. examination, he admitted that his son Jahangir is affiliated to a political party. He denied the suggestion that Mahima was noteraped and that she committed suicide due to family reasons and that she was of immoral character. 

 19. It may be stated, at this juncture that although this witness deposed to have heard narration of the occurrence and the subsequent events from the informant, his wife and two daughters, none of those witnesses admit in their deposition that PW 2 visited their house nor that they told PW 2 about the occurrence. The evidence of PW 2 with regard to the occurrence and subsequent events is, therefore, inadmissible. 

 22. This evidence being totally inadmissible, we refrain from further discussion of the same. 

 25. PW 7, Md Abdul Wahed and PW 10, Abdul Mannan, both stated in their examination-in- chief that they heard about the occurrence from the informant (PW 1) and went on to narrate what they had heard. However, PW 1 did not mention the presence of PW 7 or PW 10 at his house, nor about narrating the occurrence to them and, therefore, the evidence of PWs 7 and 10, being inadmissible as hearsay, need not be discussed any further so far as it relates to the narration of the occurrence of rape. PW 7 further stated that he heard about the accused and their father visiting the house of the informant but this is also hearsay. PW 7 admitted his presence at the time of the inquest and identified his signature in the inquest report which is marked as Exhibit 3/1. He was also a witness to the seizure list by which the wearing apparel of Mahima had been seized by the police and identified his signature thereon which is marked as Exhibit 4/1. 

 39. PW 21, Md Sanaullah, the Investigating Officer stated in his examination-in-chief that on 19-2-2002 the Thana Health Officer filed a written complaint giving details of one Mahima Khatun who was admitted in the hospital after taking poison and died at 12-50 PM. Thereafter the Officer-in-charge filed UD Case No, 4 dated 19-2-2002 at 13- 30 and handed over the investigation to him. He then prepared the inquest report and being suspicious about the cause of death sent the body for post mortem examination. He visited the place of occurrence, prepared the sketch map and index and arrested first information report named accused Uzzal. He also stated that on 20-2-2002 he seized an indistinct colour photograph from the house of accused Faroque and a plastic container for film, On 21-2-2002 he seized the Salwar and Kamiz which was tom in the back in two places. He also deposed with regard to the seizure of a negative and photograph from the house of accused Jahangir Alam (who, in fact, is not an accused in this case). The witness produced the inquest report marked Exhibit 3 and identified his signature thereon marked Exhibit 3/2. He sent the Salwar Kamiz for chemical examination and also the negative and photograph for examination by the photographic expert. He was also assigned the investigation of UD Case No.4 of 2002 dated 19-2-2002 for which he filed a final report on 5-3-2002 after obtaining the post mortem examination report and reports of the photographic expert and chemical examiner. He submitted charge sheet No. 29 dated 4-3-2002 against the accused persons. In his cross-examination he stated that Mahima's face cannot be seen in the photographs produced at the trial. He further stated that no injuries could be seen on the body of the deceased at the time of inquest. The matemal grandmother of the deceased examined the dead body, but he himself did not examine the private parts of the victim. He stated that PW 5 Jahangir stated in his statement under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (the Code) that he reached home at 10-00 PM and his mother told him about the occurrence after his meal and a little later his father came home. He also stated that PW 6 Rahima stated in her statement under section 161 of the Code that her father returned home at 9-00 PM when her mother narrated the occurrence to him and that in her 161 statement Sanowara (PW 8) stated that her husband reached home at 9-00 PM when she told him about the occurrence and that he went out after his meal., But there is no mention of her having narrated the occurrence to Jahangir. He further stated that he seized the Salwar Kamiz wom by the victim at the time of occurrence on production by the informant, but the informant did not tell him that the Salwar Kamiz has semen stain. He stated that when the negatives were printed two indistinct persons can be seen but Mahima's photograph was not found. He admitted that ex-Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina questioned him about his case. He denied the suggestion that in actual fact he found on investigation that the rape case is false. He denied the suggestion that he prepared the evidence in the case while sitting at the police station and that Mahima had an affair with a boy and being unsuccessful in that affair she committed suicide by taking poison. He stated that PW 6 Fahima did not state in her statement under section 161 of the Code that accused Uzzal said that they could now produce blue film. He also stated that PW 8 Sanowara did not state in her statement under section 161 of the Code that there were 7/8 marks on Mahima's body nor that Mahima's father asked her about the occurrence nor that at night Mannan/ Wahed came to their house. He also stated that PW 3 did not state in his statement under section 161 of the Code about Mahima telling him specifically the names of the accused. He stated that PW 5 did not state in his statement under section 161 of the Code that the accused came to their house and shouted at and rebuked his father, but did state that the accused persons used abusive language. The witness denied the suggestion that he filed a whimsical charge sheet without properly investigating the case. In his further cross-examination he stated that accused Selim. Faroque and Uzzal are college students, but did not know whether they are affiliated with Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP). 

 40. Although the charge was framed under sections 7/9(3) of the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, 1995, upon considering the evidence and materials on record, the learned trial Judge convicted all the accused persons under sections 7/9(2) of the Ain and sentenced them as stated above. 

 41. We have heard the submissions of the learned Advocates and perused the evidence and material on record. Admittedly, as is normal in this type of case, there is no direct evidence of the occurrence of rape. It has also been found and there is no dispute that the victim Mahima died in the hospital while under treatment having taken poison. The report of the chemical examiner, which is reflected in the evidence of PW 18, and the finding of the Board of doctors who conducted the post mortem examination is that the death of the victim was due to cardio-respiratory failure from organo-phosphorus compound poisoning. However, the finding of the medical board that there were marks of injury found on the dead body as mentioned in the post mortem report and that in their opinion the victim had been subjected to rape is strongly contested by the defence. The learned Advocate for the appellant has submitted that the fact of any injury upon the body of the victim Mahima was never mentioned at any stage from the time of the occurrence of the alleged rape to the time of the death of the victim, although the victim allegedly narrated the whole story to her parents and sibling. In particular her mother and younger sister would have been told about the injuries had she received any such injuries at the c time of the occurrence. Moreover, it is pointed out that no injuries were found at the time of the inquest. We find from the evidence of the doctors and the post mortem report that echymosed injuries were found on the inner middle and upper left and right thighs of the victim as well as bite marks on her right breast and scratch abrasion on her left breast. This, along with the finding of congestion in the vulva and vagina, which were also found bruised and oedematous, and the hymen ruptured, led to the opinion of the doctors that there were positive findings of forceful sexual act and assault on her person. The learned Advocate for the appellant strenuously submitted that the report of the post mortem examination and the evidence of the doctors can only be used as corroborative evidence and cannot be substantive evidence and hence, when there is no allegation of any injury on the person of the victim, the finding of injury by the medical board cannot be taken into consideration. Indeed, the learned Advocate argued that the finding of injury is false and concocted. In this regard, we are of the view that there is no indication in the records as to why the doctors would falsify their finding and produce a concocted report with regard to injuries found on a dead person. The evidence on record does not disclose any reason for the doctors to be telling lies. On the other hand, we accept the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant that the evidence of the doctors and the report of the post mortem examination cannot be substantive evidence, but can only be corroborative evidence. When there is no allegation of any injury the report could not be used as corroborative evidence of the injury. However, this case is not one of an allegation of any injury. The case before us is of an allegation of rape and subsequent death of the victim. The question therefore to be answered is, whether or not the victim was abducted and raped and thereafter to ascertain and come to a finding whether the accused persons committed that rape. In addition, in the facts of the instant case, it is also to be ascertained whether the evidence discloses the ingredients under section 9(3) of the Ain. The finding of injuries which have been reported by the doctors only goes towards the assessment as to whether or not the victim was raped and, therefore, we do not consider the finding of injuries per se, rather we look to see whether the injuries are at all material for the finding of rape. We note from the inquisition report that the victim was fully clothed at the time of the inquest and, therefore, it is expected that injuries on the lower and upper parts of the thigh of the victim as well as those on her breasts would not be visible and hence that would explain why the injuries were not seen at the time of inquest. The learned Deputy Attorney-General argued, and we accept, that the whole scenario is such that the girl was traumatised and ashamed of what has happened to her and it is not likely that she would have narrated her injuries to her relatives; she is a teen-aged girl. We, therefore, find that on the basis of the post mortem report and the evidence of the medical board the fact that the victim was raped is established beyond doubt. 

 42. The question remains, as to whether the accused persons committed the rape upon the victim. As we have stated earlier, there is neither direct ocular evidence nor any circumstantial evidence in this case to connect the accused persons with the occurrence of rape on the victim. However, it appears that the victim came home straight after the occurrence and narrated the occurrence to her sister just before dusk, to her mother just after dusk, to her brother when he returned home at about 8:00 PM and to her father when he returned home at about 9-00 PM. She also narrated the story to PW 3 at 8-00 AM on the following morning. 

 43. At this juncture, we may deal with the evidence of PWs 2, 7 and 10 so far as it relates to the occurrence of rape of the victim, It appears that PWs 2, 7 and 10 heard about the occurrence from PW 1 the informant, but PW 1 did not mention their presence or having told them about the occurrence, This evidence being hearsay of a hearsay is inadmissible in law and should not have been recorded at all and, as such, the evidence of PWs 2, 7 and 10 are left out of consideration so far as the occurrence of the rape is concerned. PW 3 was told of the occurrence by PW 8, the wife of the informant, and this is corroborated by PW 8 herself. Moreover, it is seen from the evidence of PW 3 that he himself asked the victim who cried and narrated the occurrence to him including the fact that the accused took her to Bakkar's sugarcane field at the point of choral knife and raped her one after another. Thus we have the evidence of PWs 1, 3, 5, 6 and 8 that the victim narrated the occurrence of rape to them, including the names of the accused persons as the rapists. The learned Advocate for the appellant has submitted that this evidence is hearsay since the victim did not give evidence and is, therefore, to be left out of consideration as being inadmissible. In this regard the learned Deputy Attorney-General has referred to the decision showing that hearsay evidence is admissible in certain cases as provided by the Evidence Act. Reference has been made to the decision in the SM Qamruzzaman case (cited above) that hearsay evidence is admissible to prove that the statement was made but not to prove the contents of the statement itself. 

 44. At this juncture we may consider the rule of hearsay. A fundamental rule in the law of evidence is that in any given case the evidence must be direct and to that extent the rule against hearsay is an exclusionary rule. The hearsay rule excludes evidence because the evidence given in Court is not direct evidence. The main reason for excluding such evidence inter alia is that the person who is said to have made the statement is not before the Court and cannot be subjected to cross-examination and thus the veracity of that statement could not be tested. It is argued that, therefore, the defence would be at a disadvantage. JD Heydon in his book "Evidence Cases and Materials", Second Edition, writes as follows: 

 "There are certainly dangers springing from the absence of cross-examination, but perhaps the unreliability is not so great as to justify an all embracing exclusionary rule", (Page 308). He goes on to say, "The rule is unjust where it excludes hearsay evidence of a person who is dead, or unavailable, or unidentifiable. It means that a case will be decided without taking into account all the available evidence, imperfect though some of it may be." 

 45. It is gainsay that direct evidence is the best evidence. Hearsay evidence is excluded from consideration in a case because it is not subject to cross-examination and its veracity cannot be tested causing disadvantage to the defence. At Common law there is "the best evidence rule", In Cross on Evidence, 4th Edition, page 14, it is written, "The classic statement of the best evidence rule is that of Lord Hardwicke when he said that 'the judges and sages of the law have laid it down that there is but one general rule of evidence, the best that the nature of the case will allow", But then there are other rules such as the hearsay rule which exclude evidence by way of statement made by a person who is himself not giving evidence in the proceedings. Such evidence is inadmissible as evidence of any fact stated. However, the common law provides exceptions to the hearsay rule, which have been incorporated in our Evidence Act. This may be found in sections 32 and 157 of the Evicence Act. Our rules of evidence as stated earlier are based on the English common law rules, with certain modifications. Over the years the common law rules excluding hearsay evidence have been found to be too stringent and, in certain cases, unjust and as a result a Law Commission was set up in England to investigate this matter. The Law Commission, upon scrutiny of the existing law, concluded that the rules excluding evidence that are potentially relevant and reliable were not sound in the late 20th century. They indicated that hearsay evidence sometimes tends to be the best evidence actually available, for example, when the maker of the statement died or could not be found. In such circumstances, the person to whom the statement was made would be the witness with the best evidence available. The culmination of the Law Commission's report was the enactment of the Criminal Justice Act, 2003 where section 116 makes admissible a statement not made in oral evidence in the proceedings, if the evidence of that person would have been admissible as evidence in that matter and the relevant person is dead. Similarly, in the USA the Rules of Evidence have been formulated in such a way that hearsay evidence of "spontaneous or excited utterances" would be admissible, i.e. "A statement relating to a startling event or condition made while the declarant was under the stress of excitement caused by the event Or condition" This is founded on one of the English Common Law exceptions to the hearsay rule. Such evidence is admissible upon the reasoning that the report is made at a time when the maker of the statement was under such stress that there would have been no time for reflection and no opportunity for concoction. In the light of these rules, the Superior Courts in the US have held that the statement made by a 3-year old child to her mother and later to the doctor about the indecent assault upon her by the accused is admissible. 

 46. We, therefore, find that the hearsay rule is not an absolute exclusionary rule and that the source of the rule, namely the English common law, has been modified to incorporate further inroads to find more exceptions in order to admit evidence which might otherwise be excluded by strict operation to the hearsay rule. 

 47. Going to the back of the facts of the instant case we find that the evidence shows that PW 8, the mother of the victim, found her daughters crying when she returned home and the victim narrated the occurrence to her. PW 5 also stated that the victim embraced his neck and cried and then told him about the occurrence. Similarly, PW 3 stated that on the following morning when he came to the house of the informant at 8-00 AM the victim cried and told him that the accuseds raped her one after another. Here we find direct evidence as well as hear- say evidence. The fact of the witnesses deposing regarding the victim crying is direct evidence and relates back to the occurrence which she narrated to them. This in our mind makes the evidence admissible. It is so contemporaneous to the occurrence as to defy any notion of reflection or concoction and we find no reason why it should be disbelieved. Moreover, we find that PW 3 himself saw the accused persons and their fathers/guardians at the house of the informant at 8-00/9-00 AM on Sunday. This is direct evidence and it relates back to the statement of the PWs. 1, 5, 6 and 8 that the informant went to the house of the accused to meet their parents and lodged his complaint and they returned to his house (informant's house) full of abuse and threats. This, in our mind, is further connection of the accused with the occurrence. 

 48. In view of our discussion above, we find that the accused persons have been rightly found guilty of having committed the offence of rape on victim Mahima. However, we do not find that the cause of her death was either the rape or any subsequent act of the rapists and hence, the conviction under section 9(2) of the Ain is not sustainable. There being sufficient evidence of the accused persons having committed rape on the victim they ought to have been convicted under section 9(1) of the Ain. Accordingly, we find the accused persons, namely Md Farid, Md Kamrul Hasan aiias Faroque, Md Selim Hossain and Uzzal alias Elias Hossain guilty under section 9( 1) of the Nari-o-Shishu Nirjatan Daman Ain, 2003 and sentence them to imprisonment for life and to pay fine of Taka 25,000 each, in default to suffer rigorous imprisonment for 6(six) months more.
